content: The text provided appears to be a long list of references and contributors related to studies, guidelines, and research on sexually transmitted infections (STIs), partner notification, and public health strategies. 1. Gorbach PM, Aral SO, Celum C, Stoner BP, Whittington WL, Galea J, et al. conducted a study in Seattle to explore the perspectives of patients with sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) regarding partner notification. This research was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 2. Cavalcante EG, Miranda MC, Carvalho AZ, Lima IC, and Galvao MT examined partner notification practices for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and the perceptions of notified partners. Their findings were published in a peer-reviewed journal. 3. Maman S, Mbwambo J, Hogan NM, Kilonzo GP, and Sweat M investigated the barriers women face in HIV-1 testing and disclosure, highlighting challenges in voluntary counseling and testing programs. This study was published in AIDS Care. 4. Tomnay JE, Hulme-Chambers A, Bilardi J, Fairley CK, Huffam S, and Chen MY conducted a qualitative study in Australia to identify ways to improve partner notification following an HIV diagnosis among men who have sex with men. The findings were published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs. 5. Temple-Smith M, Hopkins C, Fairley C, Tomnay J, Pavlin N, Parker R, et al. explored patients' views and experiences of informing partners about chlamydia infections. This study was published in Family Practice. 6. Temkin E, Klassen AC, Mmari K, and Gillespie DG conducted a qualitative study on the use of expedited partner therapy by patients. Their research was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 7. Mimiaga MJ, Reisner SL, Tetu AM, Bonafide KE, Cranston K, Bertrand T, et al. investigated the knowledge, attitudes, and experiences of men who have sex with men in Massachusetts regarding partner notification after STD and HIV exposures. This study was published in Public Health Reports. 8. Nuwaha F, Faxelid E, Neema S, Eriksson C, and Hojer B conducted qualitative research in Uganda to identify psychosocial determinants influencing sexual partner referral. Their findings were published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 9. Cunningham SD, Meyers T, Kerrigan D, and Ellen JM examined psychosocial factors that affect the disclosure of STI diagnoses among female adolescents. This study was published in Sexual Health. 10. Clark JL, Perez-Brumer AG, Segura ER, Salvatierra HJ, Sanchez J, and Lama JR conducted a mixed-methods analysis in Lima, Peru, to study anticipated partner notification following STD diagnoses among men who have sex with men and transgender women. The findings were published in PLOS One. 11. John SA, Walsh JL, Cho YI, and Weinhardt LS explored the perceived risk of intimate partner violence among STI clinic patients and its implications for partner notification and patient-delivered partner therapy. This study was published in Archives of Sexual Behavior. 12. Rosenfeld EA, Marx J, Terry MA, Stall R, Pallatino C, Borrero S, et al. conducted a qualitative study on intimate partner violence, partner notification, and expedited partner therapy. Their findings were published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 13. Hopkins CA, Temple-Smith MJ, Fairley CK, Pavlin NL, Tomnay JE, Parker RM, et al. investigated the acceptability of new technologies for notifying partners about chlamydia infections. This study was published in BMC Infectious Diseases. 14. Wood JM, Harries J, Kalichman M, Kalichman S, Nkoko K, and Mathews C conducted a qualitative study in South Africa to explore motivations and barriers to partner notification for STIs. Their findings were published in BMC Public Health. 15. McBride K, Goldsworthy RC, and Fortenberry JD designed and evaluated informational materials and packaging for patient-delivered partner therapy. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections. 16. Nanhoe AC, Watzeels A, and Gotz HM studied patient-initiated partner treatment for chlamydia infections in the Netherlands, focusing on the views of patients and notified partners. Their findings were published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 17. Updated recommendations for the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and syphilis, as well as new guidelines on syphilis testing and partner services, were published in a comprehensive report. 18. Nanhoe AC, Visser M, Omlo JJ, Watzeels A, van den Broek IV, and Gotz HM conducted a mixed-methods study among sexual health care providers in the Netherlands to evaluate the feasibility of providing medication for partners through chlamydia patients. This study was published in BMC Infectious Diseases. 19. Iturrieta-Guaita NG, Temple-Smith MJ, and Tomnay J explored the use of electronic communication technologies to improve syphilis partner notification in Chile. This qualitative case study was published in Sexual Health. 20. Armbruster B, Helleringer S, Kalilani-Phiri L, Mkandawire J, and Kohler HP analyzed the relative costs of contact tracing to enhance HIV case finding in sub-Saharan Africa. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 21. Cherutich P, Farquhar C, Wamuti B, Otieno FA, Ng’ang’a A, Mutiti PM, et al. conducted a cost and budget impact analysis of HIV partner services in Kenya. Their findings were published in BMC Health Services Research. 22. Clarke J, White KA, and Turner K explored short-term responses to changes in chlamydia control strategies using computational and mathematical modeling. This study was published in Computational and Mathematical Methods in Medicine. 23. Gift TL, Gaydos CA, Kent CK, Marrazzo JM, Rietmeijer CA, Schillinger JA, et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of screening men for chlamydia to prevent pelvic inflammatory disease in women. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 24. Gunn RA, Weinberg MS, Borntrager D, and Murray PJ adapted a syphilis model service for partner notification among individuals with chronic hepatitis B virus infection. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 25. Johnson BL, Tesoriero J, Feng W, Qian F, and Martin EG conducted a cost analysis and performance assessment of partner services for HIV and STDs in New York State. This study was published in Health Services Research. 26. Li XC, Kusi L, Marak T, Bertrand T, Chan PA, and Galarraga O evaluated the cost and cost-utility of three public health HIV case-finding strategies in Rhode Island. This study was published in AIDS and Behavior. 27. Macke BA, Hennessy MH, and McFarlane M identified predictors of time spent on partner notification across four U.S. sites. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections. 28. Nichols BE, Gotz HM, van Gorp EC, Verbon A, Rokx C, Boucher CA, et al. used mathematical modeling to assess the cost-effectiveness of partner notification for reducing HIV-1 transmission among men who have sex with men. This study was published in PLOS One. 29. Rahman MM, Khan M, and Gruber D developed a low-cost partner notification strategy for controlling STDs in Louisiana. This case study was published in the American Journal of Public Health. 30. Reynolds SL, Kapadia AS, Leonard L, and Ross MW examined the direct costs and effectiveness of syphilis detection through selective screening and partner notification. This study was published in the Journal of Public Health Medicine. 31. Roberts TE, Tsourapas A, Sutcliffe L, Cassell J, and Estcourt C conducted a cost-consequence analysis of Accelerated Partner Therapy (APT) as an alternative to routine patient referral for partner notification in the UK. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections. 32. Rutstein SE, Brown LB, Biddle AK, Wheeler SB, Kamanga G, and Mmodzi P evaluated the cost-effectiveness of provider-based HIV partner notification in urban Malawi. This study was published in Health Policy and Planning. 33. Sharma M, Smith JA, Farquhar C, Ying R, Cherutich P, and Golden M, et al. demonstrated that assisted partner notification services are cost-effective for reducing HIV burden in western Kenya. This study was published in AIDS. 34. Shrestha RK, Sansom SL, Kimbrough L, Hutchinson AB, Daltry D, Maldonado W, et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of using social networks to identify undiagnosed HIV infections among minority populations. This study was published in the Journal of Public Health Management and Practice. 35. Silverman RA, Katz DA, Levin C, Bell TR, Spellman D, St. John L, et al. analyzed the costs, resources, and strategies for STD partner services across jurisdictions to address unique epidemic characteristics and rising incidence rates. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 36. Turner K, Adams E, Grant A, Macleod J, Bell G, Clarke J, et al. conducted an economic and mathematical modeling study to evaluate the costs and cost-effectiveness of various chlamydia screening and partner notification strategies. This study was published in BMJ. 37. Welte R, Kretzschmar M, Leidl R, van den Hoek A, Jager JC, and Postma MJ assessed the cost-effectiveness of population-based chlamydia screening programs using a dynamic approach. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 38. Althaus CL, Turner KM, Mercer CH, Auguste P, Roberts TE, Bell G, et al. evaluated the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of traditional and new partner notification technologies for curable STIs through observational studies, systematic reviews, and mathematical modeling. This study was published in Health Technology Assessment. 39. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed a training curriculum for healthcare providers to care for women subjected to violence, including intimate partner violence and sexual violence. This curriculum is available through WHO's official publications. 40. WHO also published clinical and policy guidelines for responding to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women, providing evidence-based recommendations for healthcare providers.
